clinicalPearls: Mastocytosis is defined by accumulation of clonally expanded mast cells in tissues (skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen, gut); mast cell expansion is most readily identified in skin and/or bone marrow (p.2819).
More than 90% of patients carry a somatic gain-of-function KIT D816V mutation in the stem cell factor receptor gene (p.2819).

Classification recognizes cutaneous mastocytosis (with variants), systemic mastocytosis (SM, five variants), and mast cell sarcoma; cutaneous mastocytosis is the most common diagnosis in children and is usually diagnosed within the first year of life (p.2819-2820).

Systemic mastocytosis denotes involvement of an extracutaneous site, most often bone marrow; indolent systemic mastocytosis (ISM) accounts for >70% of adult patients and is associated with a normal life expectancy (p.2820).

Cutaneous lesions of maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (MPCM, also called urticaria pigmentosa) are reddish-brown macules, papules, or plaques that urticate and become erythematous on rubbing or trauma (Darier's sign) (p.2820).

Clinical manifestations of SM reflect release of bioactive mast cell mediators plus tissue infiltration: intermittent urticaria, flushing, tachycardia and vascular collapse, gastric acid hypersecretion, crampy lower abdominal pain, and diarrhea (p.2820).

Anaphylaxis in mastocytosis is most commonly triggered by Hymenoptera stings and NSAIDs; symptom flares may also follow alcohol, temperature change, stress, and mast cell-interactive opioids (p.2820).
A basal serum tryptase level is a useful noninvasive test to consider before bone marrow biopsy; total serum tryptase >20 ng/mL is a minor diagnostic criterion for SM (p.2821).

Diagnosis of SM requires tissue confirmation (lesional/bone marrow biopsy): one major plus one minor, or three minor criteria. Major = multifocal dense mast cell aggregates (>15 mast cells per aggregate) in extracutaneous tissue; minor = spindled/atypical morphology, aberrant CD25/CD2/CD30 phenotype, activating KIT mutation, or tryptase >20 ng/mL (p.2821).

Patients with recurrent mast cell activation (especially anaphylaxis with hypotensive syncope) who carry KIT D816V but do not meet full SM criteria are termed monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome (p.2821).
harrison.pathophysiology: Mastocytosis is a clonal mast cell disorder driven by somatic gain-of-function mutations in the KIT (stem cell factor receptor) gene, with KIT D816V present in >90% of patients. The mutation produces ligand-independent KIT activation and clonal mast cell proliferation/accumulation in skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen, and gut. KIT mutations occur across all forms of SM and in lesional skin of some children with cutaneous disease; additional mutations (TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1, RUNX1) seen in other hematologic neoplasms can appear in advanced SM variants. Disease manifestations arise from release of bioactive mast cell mediators acting locally and distally, tissue infiltration by mast cells, and the tissue response to that infiltrate; mast cell-mediated fibrosis may affect liver, spleen, and bone marrow but not gastrointestinal tissue or skin (p.2819-2820).
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (autosomal dominant extra copies of the alpha-tryptase gene at TPSAB1; elevated baseline serum tryptase with multisystem mast cell activation symptoms)
Recurrent IgE-mediated or idiopathic anaphylaxis (usually presents with urticaria, angioedema and/or bronchospasm, which are not typical manifestations of anaphylaxis in SM)
additionalInvestigations: Basal (baseline) serum tryptase as a noninvasive screen before bone marrow biopsy
Bone marrow biopsy with mast cell morphology, immunophenotype (CD25, CD2, CD30), and KIT D816V mutation testing for systemic disease
Skin biopsy to confirm diffuse cutaneous and bullous mastocytosis subvariants
24-h urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (carcinoid) and metanephrines (pheochromocytoma) to exclude mimics
Bone densitometry, bone scan, or skeletal survey (osteoporosis is increased and may cause pathologic fractures)
CT scan or endoscopy and neuropsychiatric evaluation as directed by presentation
redFlags: Anaphylaxis with rapid, life-threatening vascular collapse (most often after Hymenoptera stings or NSAIDs)
Hypotensive syncope from mast cell activation

C findings of aggressive disease: cytopenias, hepatomegaly with ascites and impaired liver function, splenomegaly with hypersplenism, malabsorption with hypoalbuminemia and weight loss, or osteolytic skeletal lesions with pathologic fractures
Circulating atypical mast cells suggesting mast cell leukemia
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis is variant-dependent. Life expectancy is normal for cutaneous mastocytosis and most ISM; progression from ISM to a more advanced form is uncommon (~5% lifetime risk). In SM-AHNMD, outcome is determined by the associated non-mast cell hematologic disorder. SSM carries an intermediate prognosis. Aggressive SM and mast cell leukemia have a poor prognosis, and mast cell leukemia is invariably fatal at present. In infants and children with cutaneous disease, visceral involvement is usually absent and spontaneous resolution before adolescence is common; progression from cutaneous mastocytosis to ISM occurs in ~10% of children, especially with high mast cell burden or hematologic abnormalities (p.2820).
pitfalls: Atopy is not increased in mastocytosis compared with the general population (p.2819).
Imatinib is not effective in most cases because the KIT D816V mutation confers resistance (p.2821).
Osteoporosis alone without osteolytic lesions does not satisfy the C-finding skeletal criterion for aggressive SM (p.2821).
SM cannot be confirmed on clinical and laboratory grounds alone; tissue diagnosis is required (p.2821).
Anaphylaxis in SM typically lacks the urticaria, angioedema, and bronchospasm seen in IgE-mediated or idiopathic anaphylaxis (p.2821).
Baseline serum tryptase elevation must be interpreted with caution where hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (extra TPSAB1 copies) coexists (p.2821).
harrison.severityClassification: Consensus classification: Cutaneous mastocytosis (CM) - maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (MPCM/urticaria pigmentosa), solitary mastocytoma of skin, diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis. Systemic mastocytosis (SM) - indolent SM (ISM, >70% of adults, normal life expectancy), smoldering SM (SSM; >=2 B findings, no C findings: high mast cell burden with marrow infiltration >30%, basal tryptase >200 ng/mL, and/or KIT D816V VAF >10%, dysmyelopoiesis, organomegaly), SM with associated clonal hematologic non-mast cell lineage disease (SM-AHNMD), aggressive SM (ASM; >=1 C finding - cytopenias, hepatic dysfunction with ascites, hypersplenism, malabsorption with weight loss, osteolytic fractures), mast cell leukemia (MCL, rarest, invariably fatal). Mast cell sarcoma (MCS) is a rare invasive solid mast cell tumor (Tables 366-1, 366-2; p.2820).
management: Avoid known mediator-release triggers and provide self-injectable adrenaline with a written anaphylaxis plan
Symptom control with H1- and H2-antihistamines, mast cell stabilisers (sodium cromoglicate) and leukotriene antagonists, with H2-blockers or proton pump inhibitors for gastric acid hypersecretion
Topical corticosteroids or phototherapy for symptomatic cutaneous disease
Bone density surveillance with bisphosphonate therapy for the associated osteoporosis and fracture risk
For advanced systemic disease, KIT-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors (midostaurin, avapritinib) and cytoreductive therapy, guided by KIT D816V status
In systemic mastocytosis with an associated haematological neoplasm, treat the associated disorder, which determines outcome
Monitor with serial tryptase and assessment for progression, involving haematology and allergy specialists
